summary: Sets out technical criteria for choosing the Next Generation of IP. It was part of the IPng selection effort and is informational.

eli5.summary: A list of what the new internet address system must be good at, so the designers can pick the best.

questions: what are the criteria for ipv6
subtitle: Technical requirements and evaluation criteria for the next generation of IP

tldr.problem: The IETF needed a comprehensive set of criteria to evaluate and choose among competing IPng proposals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists seventeen technical requirements organized by priority and timeline, plus design principles, routing requirements, and explicit exclusions of what IPng should not require.
tldr.outcome: These criteria guided the eventual selection of IPv6 and remain a model for how the IETF evaluates major protocol decisions.

today: RFC 1726 is Informational and documents the criteria that guided the selection of IPv6 as IPng. IPv6 was designed to satisfy these criteria and remains in deployment today, though many criteria like ubiquitous mobility and full QoS support continue to evolve. The criteria document remains a reference for how major protocol decisions should be evaluated.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This RFC was commissioned by the IETF's IPng area to create a clear list of criteria for evaluating IPng proposals. The criteria come from many sources: prior proposals, IESG deliberations, academic papers, working group meetings, and community discussion. The document is deliberately framed as goals and requirements rather than specific engineering solutions.

The RFC establishes design philosophy with five guiding principles: Architectural Simplicity (IP should be the waist of the hourglass, not doing too much); One Protocol to Bind Them All (global IP connectivity is essential, but multi-protocol operation is allowed); Live Long (IPng should last 10-15+ years without major revision); Live Long AND Prosper (it must offer new benefits, not just fix IPv4's limitations); and Cooperative Anarchy (preserve the Internet's decentralized nature with minimal forced cooperation).
sections.eli5: IPng should be simple, bind the internet together globally, last a very long time, offer things IPv4 cannot do, and not require everyone to obey one central rule.

sections.title: Core Technical Requirements
sections.content:
Scale is the motivating problem: IPng must address at least 10^12 end systems and 10^9 individual networks, with routing that scales at less than the square root of the number of networks. Topological Flexibility requires support for many different network topologies; the internet will not remain tree-shaped, and hierarchies may be very tall, very short, or very broad.

Performance demands that state-of-the-art commercial routers and hosts process IPng as efficiently as IPv4, keeping up with media speeds that will grow from ones of bits per second to hundreds of gigabits per second. Robust Service requires the protocol to behave gracefully with malformed packets, misconfigurations, and failures, protecting general users from individual sites' mistakes. Media Independence means IPng must work across all LAN, MAN, and WAN media without requiring global standardization of any single mechanism.

Unreliable Datagram Service preserves IPv4's powerful property that any datagram can be thrown away without warning, and that any router can be turned off without disruption. This vastly simplifies the protocol and enhances robustness. Unique Naming ensures every endpoint has a globally unique identifier that persists across topological changes, enabling accounting and addressing simultaneously.
sections.eli5: IPng must support trillions of devices, many network shapes, fast routers, graceful handling of mistakes, work over any media, keep the simple datagram idea, and give every device a unique name.

sections.title: Protocol Features and Evolution
sections.content:
Transition from IPv4 must be straightforward. There cannot be a flag-day cutover; IPv4 and IPng must coexist for years, with mechanisms for hosts to support both, for conversion between protocols, or for backward-compatible extensions. IPv4 hosts will likely exist forever, and IPng must enable them to communicate with IPng hosts afterward.

Extensibility allows IPng to evolve without network-wide upgrades. Algorithms, headers, data structures, and packet types should be extensible so new features can be added and incrementally deployed. Control Protocol must include elementary support for testing (like ICMP's ping and traceroute) but should return more datagram data than IPv4's ICMP, which only includes 64 bits.

Configuration, Administration, and Operation must permit automatic host and router configuration. Nodes must discover routers dynamically and obtain operational parameters at boot. While full plug-and-play is beyond IPng's scope, IPng must not prevent it. Address allocation must be easy, and the system must work on isolated subnets without routers.
sections.eli5: IPng must evolve, switch over smoothly from IPv4, include debugging tools, and let machines configure themselves automatically without a central administrator.

sections.title: Advanced Capabilities
sections.content:
Secure Operation requires authentication of sources, protection of routing operations, denial-of-service defenses, and traffic-pattern confidentiality. Security must be integral from the start. Multicast capability must support both unicast and multicast, including the ability to send to all hosts on a subnet, and dynamic routing of multicast groups up to 10^6 participants. Unlike IPv4, IPng should not send to all hosts on a subnet when targeting only IPng hosts.

Network Service allows the network to associate packets with service classes and provide specified quality of service. This includes policy-based routing, flows, resource reservation, and the ability to specify costs. Real-time, mission-critical applications must be supported within IPng's datagram model. Support for Mobility is essential as devices increasingly move: hosts must remain connected while physically moving (with sessions open) and must be able to disconnect and reconnect at new network locations. Mobile networks (like ships) and mobile internetworks (ships carrying aircraft) must both work.

Private Networks enable research communities to build overlay networks and allow non-IP islands (like CLNP networks) to interconnect over the Internet using tunneling.
sections.eli5: IPng adds security, multicast for group communication, quality-of-service for multimedia, support for portable devices and ships, and the ability to build private networks on top of it.

sections.title: Design Architecture and Standards
sections.content:
Access requires that all IPng specifications be published as standard-track RFCs freely available without licensing fees, following the Internet tradition that open standards enable innovation. Routing deserves special attention because it is deeply intertwined with addressing, scale, and service delivery. The routing architecture must scale to 10^9 to 10^12 networks; support policy-based routing where networks can set their own traffic policies; propagate service quality information; provide feedback to users about available routes; remain stable even when considering multiple factors like policies and service grades; and dynamically build multicast routes based on membership and requested services.

The RFC explicitly lists things IPng should NOT require: fragmentation (path MTU discovery suffices), IP header checksums (datalink CRC and TCP checksums provide adequate protection), specific firewall support, network management (that belongs in SNMP and MIBs), accounting infrastructure (it should support cost parameters but accounting belongs in separate protocols), or specific routing protocols. These design choices keep IPng focused on its core mission.
sections.eli5: IPng's specifications must be free and open. Routing must scale enormously and handle policies and quality-of-service. IPng deliberately skips some features so other protocols can handle them better.

sections.title: Implementation Timeline
sections.content:
The RFC assigns timeframes to different criteria to guide development. Requirements like scale, topological flexibility, robust service, unreliable datagram service, unique naming, and access must be immediately demonstrable. Configuration and operation on small subnets and core control-protocol functions are required immediately. Media independence specifications for currently standardized media are needed immediately, with guidelines for future encapsulations.

Some features have medium-term timeframes: transition plans are required immediately but completion is ongoing; network service (QoS) should be available within 24 months; dynamic multicast routing within 18 months; and mobility frameworks within a year. Security should be integral from the start. This timeline reflects the authors' judgment that major IP changes happen only once per decade, and all critical features should be designed from the beginning even if some take time to implement fully.
sections.eli5: Some things must work immediately, others can take 18 months to a year. This makes sure designers think about everything from day one even if some features ship later.
